---
title: "Puyallup Conservation Measures & Proposals"
output: github_document
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(message=FALSE, warning=FALSE)
```

This is an exploratory analysis of one idea I have to test for hybridization w/ introgression of White River spring run and Puyallup River fall run Chinook salmon. It is based on a 2-sample permutation test of FST estimates of White River spring run and Puyallup River fall run from different time points. To demonstrate the test, I simulate genetic data sampled at 3 different time points: 2021, 2026, and 2031. I simulated the data so FST would decrease slightly (by chance alone) from 2021 to 2026, and then decrease extremely from 2026 to 2031 to simulate a hypothetical scenario of hybridization of White River spring run and Puyallup River fall run w/ complete introgression.         

First we import Chinook salmon genotypes from Van Doornick et al. 2024, filter the White River and Puyallup River samples, edit the sample labels, and convert the format so we can estimate FST with `pegas`.  


```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(pegas)

loci <- 
  read.loci(file="../../Chinook/loci.txt") |>
  filter(population %in% c("White_R_H_DFW", "Puyallup_R_DFW")) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(population=as.character(population) |> gsub(pattern="\\w{4}$", replacement="") |> factor()) |>
  as.loci()

loci

table(loci$population)
```
We see there are 94 fish in the Puyallup R sample and 91 fish in the White R sample.  

Lets randomly divide this data into 2 sets. This is random but I use `set.seed` so we always get 2 datasets that I know will be quite different (I tinkered with different seeds to find one that produced different genotypes). If I didn't use `set.seed` then this result wouldn't be reproducible. 

```{r}
set.seed(7)

B <- 
  slice_sample(loci, prop=0.5, by=population)

A <- 
  anti_join(x=loci, y=B)

table(A$population); table(B$population)
```

Okay, now we have 2 datasets. The 1st dataset "A" has 47 fish in the Puyallup R sample and 46 fish in White R sample. The 2nd dataset "B" has 47 fish in the Puyallup R sample and 45 fish in White R sample. Remember, the purpose of these 2 datasets is to simulate data sampled from different time points.  

Now lets estimate FST from data at these 2 simulated timepoints. FST is estimated for each locus independently, so we'll get n=94 FST estimates. Some of these estimates will be `NA` just by chance, since there are loci with very low minor allele frequencies, they will likely be fixed in the simulated datasets.     

```{r}
Fst_A <- 
  Fst(A)[, 2] |> 
  as.double()

Fst_B <- 
  Fst(B)[, 2] |> 
  as.double()

sum(is.na(Fst_A))

sum(is.na(Fst_B))
```

We see above that 5 SNPs were fixed in the "A" data and 4 in the "B" data. One nice thing about this permutation test is that it's robust to missing data.    

Now let's take the mean of the n=94 FST estimates to get the overall FST.     

```{r}
mean(Fst_A, na.rm=TRUE)

mean(Fst_B, na.rm=TRUE)
```

These FSTs are different just by chance alone. Let's plot the distributions with the mean FST annotated below the x-axis labels.     

```{r, fig.height=8}
par(mfrow=c(2, 1))

hist(Fst_A, breaks=30, xlim=c(min(c(Fst_A, Fst_B), na.rm=TRUE)*1.2, max(c(Fst_A, Fst_B), na.rm=TRUE)*1.1), main="White R H vs. Puyallup R\n2021 (simulated)", sub=paste("mean:", mean(Fst_A, na.rm=TRUE) |> round(digits=4)), xlab=expression(italic(F)[ST]))

hist(Fst_B, breaks=20, xlim=c(min(c(Fst_A, Fst_B), na.rm=TRUE)*1.2, max(c(Fst_A, Fst_B), na.rm=TRUE)*1.1), main="White R H vs. Puyallup R\n2026 (simulated)", sub=paste("mean:", mean(Fst_B, na.rm=TRUE) |> round(digits=4)), xlab=expression(italic(F)[ST]))
```

These distributions and mean FSTs look kinda different. Are they significantly different? We need a statistical test to answer that!  

Let's define our test statistic as the difference in mean FSTs estimated at 2 different timepoints.    

```{r}
mean(Fst_B, na.rm=TRUE) - mean(Fst_A, na.rm=TRUE)
```

This is negative (by design), to simulate a noticible decrease of genetic differentiation between White R and Puyallup River that could be expected to happen by chance alone. 

Now let's generate a null distribution of our test statistic. We do this with a 4 step routine: (1) shuffle FSTs between populations, (2) compute the mean FSTs from shuffled samples, (3) compute the difference of the mean FSTs (i.e., the permuted test statistic), and (4) repeat steps 1-3 at least 1,000 times.  

```{r}
AB <- 
  c(Fst_A, Fst_B)

permute2samplet <- 
  function(x, n_loci){
    n <- n_loci*2
    idx_b <- sample(1:n, n_loci)
    idx_a <- setdiff(1:n, idx_b)
    mean_diff <- mean(x[idx_b], na.rm=TRUE) - mean(x[idx_a], na.rm=TRUE)
    return(mean_diff)}

permuteAB <- rep(NA, 1000)

set.seed(13)

for(i in 1:1000){permuteAB[i] <- permute2samplet(x=AB, n_loci=94)}
```

Okay now let's compute a non-parametric "p-value" for the test. This is simply the proportion of the permuted test statistics that are more extreme than our observed test statistic. We use the absolute values of test statistics to make it 2-tailed, since we expect both FST increases and decreases to occur in nature just by chance alone.  

```{r}
obsAB <-
  mean(Fst_B, na.rm=TRUE) - 
  mean(Fst_A, na.rm=TRUE)

par(mfrow=c(1, 1))

# 2-tailed p-value
mean(abs(c(permuteAB, obsAB)) >= abs(obsAB))

hist(c(permuteAB, obsAB), xlab=expression(italic(F)[ST]~differences), breaks=30, main=paste("p-value:", mean(abs(c(permuteAB, obsAB)) >= abs(obsAB)) |> round(digits=5)))

abline(v=obsAB, lty=2, col="blue")

```

The observed test statistic is indicated by the blue dashed line. We see a fair portion of the null distribution of the test statistic is more extreme than the observed test statistic (we know that happened just by chance alone), which is quantified by the "p-value".  

Now lets simulate a third dataset "C" that is designed to result in an extreme decrease in the FST estimate. Under the scenario of hybridization w/ introgression, the White R spring run and Puyallup R fall run would become a single population, and the distinctiveness of those 2 ancestral populations would be lost forever. Lets simulate that grim scenario by creating White and Puyallup data that is really only from the White R with half of the samples randomly labeled "Puyallup R". We could do this vice-versa and it would simulate the same scenario but I am not going to show that.  

```{r}
set.seed(2)

C1 <- 
  filter(loci, population=="White_R_H") |> 
  slice_sample(prop=0.5) |> 
  as_tibble() |> 
  mutate(population=as.character(population))

C2 <- 
  anti_join(x=filter(loci, population=="White_R_H"), y=C1) |> 
  as_tibble() |> 
  mutate(population="Puyallup_R")

C <- 
  bind_rows(C1, C2) |> 
  mutate(population=factor(population)) |>
  as.loci()

Fst_C <- 
  Fst(C)[, 2] |> 
  as.double()

mean(Fst_A, na.rm=TRUE); mean(Fst_B, na.rm=TRUE); mean(Fst_C, na.rm=TRUE)
```

We can see above that our simulated data produced the desired pattern in FST: slight decrease from t1 to t2 (e.g., 2021 to 2026) followed by an extreme decrease from t2 to t3 (e.g., 2026 to 2031). Now lets plot these distributions so we can see what that looks like.  


```{r, fig.height=12}
par(mfrow=c(3, 1))

hist(Fst_A, breaks=30, xlim=c(min(c(Fst_A, Fst_B, Fst_C), na.rm=TRUE)*1.2, max(c(Fst_A, Fst_B, Fst_C), na.rm=TRUE)*1.1), main="White R H vs. Puyallup R\n2021 (simulated)", sub=paste("mean:", mean(Fst_A, na.rm=TRUE) |> round(digits=4)), xlab=expression(italic(F)[ST]))

hist(Fst_B, breaks=20, xlim=c(min(c(Fst_A, Fst_B, Fst_C), na.rm=TRUE)*1.2, max(c(Fst_A, Fst_B, Fst_C), na.rm=TRUE)*1.1), main="White R H vs. Puyallup R\n2026 (simulated)", sub=paste("mean:", mean(Fst_B, na.rm=TRUE) |> round(digits=4)), xlab=expression(italic(F)[ST]))

hist(Fst_C, breaks=10, xlim=c(min(c(Fst_A, Fst_B, Fst_C), na.rm=TRUE)*1.2, max(c(Fst_A, Fst_B, Fst_C), na.rm=TRUE)*1.1), main="White R H vs. Puyallup R\n2031 (simulated)", sub=paste("mean:", mean(Fst_C, na.rm=TRUE) |> round(digits=4)), xlab=expression(italic(F)[ST]))
```

The pattern is clear: FST declines to zero as would be expected under the scenario of hybridization w/ introgression. Now lets run the statistical test to demonstrate how to quantify significance.  

```{r}
BC <- 
  c(Fst_B, Fst_C)

permuteBC <- rep(NA, 1000)

set.seed(13)

for(i in 1:1000){permuteBC[i] <- permute2samplet(x=BC, n_loci=94)}

obsBC <-
  mean(Fst_C, na.rm=TRUE) - 
  mean(Fst_B, na.rm=TRUE)

obsBC
```

We see our observed test statistic above indicating a big decrease in FST. We compute the non-parametric "p-value" as in the same manner as before but we see a very small value this time which indicates a significant decrease in FST from t2 to t3. 

```{r, fig.height=4}
par(mfrow=c(1, 1))

# 2-tailed p-value
mean(abs(c(permuteBC, obsBC)) >= abs(obsBC))

hist(c(permuteBC, obsBC), xlab=expression(italic(F)[ST]~differences), breaks=30, main=paste("p-value:", mean(abs(c(permuteBC, obsBC)) >= abs(obsBC)) |> round(digits=5)))

abline(v=obsBC, lty=2, col="blue")
```

It's clear in the figure above that none of the null distribution of the test statistic is more extreme than the observed test statistic (which we always include in the vector of null test statistics just to ensure our p-value doesn't compute as 0).  


I hope this example will be easy to digest. One important thing would be to run through this test with the actual reference dataset used by DFW for this system. DFW has excellent reference data for the Puyallup-White Chinook, and using larger numbers of fish, say for example n=100 in each White R spring and Puyallup R fall, to estimate FST of the full 298 SNP panel will result in much less stochasticity of FST than the toy examples I presented here, which had only 94 SNPs and about n=45 fish per population.
